extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literary students, and readers interested in story structure and narrative archetypes
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Christopher Booker's framework of the seven basic plots and related narrative principles to evaluate or create stories. Focuses on archetypal plot types, their variants, psychological functions, and common failures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overcoming the monster
rubrics_metrics.description: A basic plot in which a hero confronts and defeats a powerful, threatening force (the monster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the seven gateways; includes treatment of 'the monster (II) and the thrilling escape from death' — emphasises confrontation with external evil and the dramatic escape/resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rags to riches
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot in which a protagonist rises from poverty or low status to wealth, power, or happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of the seven basic plots; implies transformation of social/status circumstances as core narrative movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The quest
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot driven by the protagonist's journey to achieve a significant goal or obtain an important object, involving trials and companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the seven basic plots; emphasizes a series of obstacles and the protagonist's development through pursuit of the goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voyage and return
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot in which the protagonist goes to a strange world, experiences challenges, and returns changed (often wiser) to the ordinary world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed among the seven basic plots; stresses the experience of dislocation, encounter with the unfamiliar, and eventual return.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy (basic plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative form that typically moves from confusion or conflict toward reconciliation, social harmony, or a felicitous resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a basic plot and further treated in 'Comedy (II): the plot disguised' — covers both overt comic structure and disguised/comic elements within other forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy — the five stages
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy conceived as a structured progression (the 'five stages') leading to downfall; one of the principal plot types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears as 'Tragedy (I): the five stages' — book outlines stages that define tragic movement (details elaborated in the text).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy — the divided self
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant of tragedy focused on internal division within the protagonist (split self) that drives the tragic outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as 'Tragedy (II): the divided self' — emphasizes psychological conflict and internal contradictions as the source of tragic action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy — the hero as monster
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragic variant where the hero's actions transform them into something monstrous, implicating moral inversion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as 'Tragedy (III): the hero as monster' — explores how heroic traits become pathological and lead to catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebirth
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot in which a protagonist undergoes a profound transformation or moral/spiritual renewal, often following apparent death or ruin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included among the seven basic plots; linked with themes of renewal and emergence from darkness into light.

rubrics_metrics.name: The seven gateways to the underworld (structural framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: An organizing conception framing the seven basic plots as gateways to archetypal underworld experiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as the prologue to part one; treats the seven plots as connected archetypal experiences (underworld imagery/metaphor).

rubrics_metrics.name: The rule of three (role of numbers in stories)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative principle that patterns or events often occur in threes and that number plays a structural/psychological role in stories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epilogue to part 1: 'the rule of three (the role played in stories by numbers)' — discusses numeric patterns as a compositional device and archetypal resonance.

rubrics_metrics.name: The complete happy ending
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative ideal in which conflicts are resolved fully and the story culminates in a positive, balanced outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline for part two; contrasts with darker variants and analyzes components that produce a 'complete' happy ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Character types or forces in stories that embody destructive, shadow, or antagonistic values.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part two addresses 'The dark figures' as crucial oppositional elements whose resolution/containment is necessary for a full happy ending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light figures
rubrics_metrics.description: Character types that embody positive, redemptive, or integrative values; counterbalance dark figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paired with dark figures in part two; their role is to restore balance and help reach narrative goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seeing whole — feminine and masculine values
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluative criterion that stories should integrate or show the interaction of feminine and masculine values to achieve wholeness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed as 'Seeing whole: the feminine and masculine values' — suggests that balance of differing value-systems is a narrative goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: The perfect balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative state where opposing values or tendencies are reconciled, producing a harmonious outcome.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of the 'complete happy ending' discussion — stresses attaining equilibrium between competing forces/values.

rubrics_metrics.name: The unrealised value
rubrics_metrics.description: A thematic problem where a potentially positive value is neglected or unfulfilled within the story, undermining resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in part two as a concept to diagnose why stories fail to achieve proper fulfilment of their themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: The archetypal family drama
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories structured around familial relationships and archetypal family roles and conflicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appears in part two as a recurring narrative form; indicates family dynamics as central to many archetypal plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reaching the goal
rubrics_metrics.description: A plot requirement describing the protagonist's achievement of the narrative objective (or failure to do so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Reaching the goal' is discussed in part two as part of what constitutes a complete ending and successful plot movement.

rubrics_metrics.name: The fatal flaw
rubrics_metrics.description: A character defect or error (hamartia) that precipitates downfall or blocks fulfilment of the story's aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed in part two; treated as a dramatic engine (particularly in tragedy) and as a diagnostic for why characters fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Missing the mark / The ego takes over (dark inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A class of failures where the author's/characters' ego-driven distortions invert or corrupt archetypal plots, leading to 'missing the mark.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part three's theme: 'The ego takes over (I): enter the dark inversion' and subsequent sections show how ego-driven variants produce dark or sentimental distortions of basic plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dark and sentimental versions (ego distortions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants of plots produced when sentimentality or excessive darkness replace archetypal purpose, producing distorted narrative effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered in 'The ego takes over (II): the dark and sentimental versions' — explains common anti-patterns in twentieth-century storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific ego inversions (quest/voyage/comedy variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: How quest, voyage and return, and comedy forms can be corrupted when ego-driven concerns dominate, producing failed versions of those plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discussed in 'The ego takes over (III): quest, voyage and return, comedy' — identifies pattern-specific degenerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tragedy and rebirth corrupted by ego
rubrics_metrics.description: How tragic and rebirth plots are inverted when ego domination leads to loss of archetypal integrity, producing nihilistic or empty outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Covered in 'The ego takes over (IV): tragedy and rebirth' — details how such core plots can fail when disconnected from archetypal purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Losing the plot (case studies)
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagnostic rubric: stories that have 'lost the plot' by losing touch with archetypal purpose; illustrated via literary case studies (e.g., Thomas Hardy).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Losing the plot: Thomas Hardy, a case history' provides an example of how a canonical author can exemplify this failure; use as warning/example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Going nowhere — the passive ego
rubrics_metrics.description: A failure mode where narratives stagnate because passive ego orientation produces dead-end plots (twentieth-century examples from Chekhov to Close Encounters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Going nowhere: the passive ego' diagnoses stagnation as a common modern narrative problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why sex and violence? — the active ego
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanation/criterion for why modern narratives may emphasize sex and violence as manifestations of the active ego, often obsessive and reductionist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Why sex and violence?: the active ego: the twentieth-century obsession: from de Sade to The Terminator' — analyzes cultural/psychological drivers and narrative consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebellion against 'the one'
rubrics_metrics.description: A thematic/plot form where narratives depict revolt against an integrating principle or absolute (examples: Job, Nineteen Eighty-Four).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Rebellion against "the one": from Job to Nineteen eighty-four' — discusses a recurrent motif and its narrative implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: The mystery
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot element/form centering on a puzzling situation or secret that drives the narrative and demands resolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included in part three as an archetypal motif with its own rules and expectations for revealing and withholding information.

rubrics_metrics.name: The riddle of the sphinx (Oedipus and Hamlet)
rubrics_metrics.description: An archetypal motif focusing on existential riddles and the protagonist's confrontation with fate or puzzling truth (case studies: Oedipus, Hamlet).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'The riddle of the sphinx: Oedipus and Hamlet' used as exemplars of stories driven by enigmatic destiny and moral/psychological questioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Telling us who we are — ego versus instinct
rubrics_metrics.description: Criterion that stories reveal human nature by dramatizing the tension between ego (conscious self) and instinct (deeper forces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part four: 'Telling us who we are: ego versus instinct' frames storytelling as a diagnostic mirror of psychological dynamics; use to evaluate thematic depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Into the real world — the ruling consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrative consideration of how dominant consciousness/ruling perspective shapes story reality and reader alignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Into the real world: the ruling consciousness' examines whose consciousness governs the narrative and its moral/psychological stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Of gods and men — reconnecting with 'the one'
rubrics_metrics.description: A thematic criterion that stories can restore connection with an integrating principle (the 'one'), yielding transcendence or moral reconciliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Of gods and men: reconnecting with "the one"' addresses narratives that re-establish unity or higher moral order as part of resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: The age of Loki — dismantling of the self
rubrics_metrics.description: A diagnosis of modern narratives that fragment identity and undermine the cohesive self, often leading to anti-plot tendencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'The age of Loki: the dismantling of the self' critiques contemporary tendencies to deconstruct identity and their effects on narrative coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Light and the shadows on the wall (epilogue insight)
rubrics_metrics.description: Final syntheses about the interplay of illuminating and obscuring forces in stories — how light (integration) and shadow (destruction) shape meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Epilogue: the light and the shadows on the wall' functions as a summative principle for assessing a story's balance between integrative and destructive elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Archetypal purpose and psychological meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching criterion that good stories should connect to archetypal purposes and convey psychological meaning rooted in human development and evolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: From the page summary: the book 'attempts to distill all of storytelling down to a few archetypes' and 'analyzes why evolution has given us the need to tell stories' — use as meta-criterion for evaluating whether a story resonates at an archetypal/psychological level.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding loss of archetypal purpose ('lost the plot')
rubrics_metrics.description: An evaluative standard warning that many modern stories fail by losing touch with their underlying archetypal purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page notes authors 'lead readers through... why so many stories have "lost the plot" by losing touch with their underlying archetypal purpose' — treat as an anti-pattern: check whether a story maintains its archetypal function.
